You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Globally, approximately 1.3 million total joint implants are placed annually, and around 80,000 patients develop aseptic loosening, a leading cause of implant failure driven by peri-implant fibrosis. Here, we show that the BMP-antagonist Gremlin-1 (GREM1), expressed by leptin receptor–expressing skeletal (LEPR⁺) cells, is a key regulator of this process. GREM1 is highly expressed by LEPR⁺ cells in peri-implant fibrotic tissue in mice and humans. Conditional deletion of Grem1 in LEPR⁺ cells attenuate peri-implant fibrosis and enhances peri-implant osteogenesis. Transcriptomic and functional analyses show that loss of Grem1 in LEPR⁺ cells upregulate the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) and WNT pathways, increasing in vivo osteogenesis and reducing fibrous tissue formation. As proof-of-concept, intra-articular administration of a neutralizing antibody against GREM1 (anti-GREM1) in mice prevents and reverses peri-implant fibrous tissue while promoting peri-implant bone formation. Inhibition of GREM1 in LEPR⁺ cells therefore represent a promising strategy to prevent and treat aseptic loosening.

---

## Introduction

Around 1.3 million total joint implants1,2 are implanted worldwide annually for the treatment of osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis, post-traumatic arthritis, and avascular necrosis. Peri-implant fibrosis is one of the most common causes of failure in prosthetic joint implants3,4, affecting approximately 80,000 people in the United States with joint prostheses4,5. In peri-implant fibrosis, fibrous tissue forms around the implant instead of bone, preventing proper stabilization of the implant, leading to instability and pain6-8. Addressing this issue typically requires surgical revision, which involves removing the existing implant and surrounding fibrotic tissue, followed by the placement of a new implant. Unfortunately, revision surgeries are associated with significant morbidity, mortality, decreased patient-reported outcomes scores, and increased re-revision rates9-12. Therefore, identifying biological therapeutic targets that can prevent or reverse peri-implant fibrosis is a critical priority to minimize the need for revision surgeries.

We have recently demonstrated that skeletal cells expressing the leptin receptor (LEPR+) are both necessary and sufficient to induce peri-implant fibrosis13. These LEPR+ cells highly overlap with CXCL12+ cells, which are commonly referred to as CXCL12-abundant reticular (CAR) cells14. In addition to CXCL12, LEPR+ cells also express high levels of the transcription factors EBF315 and FOXC116, as well as previously reported markers of skeletal progenitors, including CD20017, PDGFRα18, and alpha-smooth muscle actin (αSMA)19. LEPR+ cells consist of multiple subtypes, including an osteogenic subtype, sometimes referred to as osteoCAR cells, characterized by the expression of alkaline phosphatase (ALPL)20 and an adipogenic subtype, sometimes referred to as adipoCAR cells or marrow adipogenic lineage precursors (MALPs), marked by the expression of adiponectin (Adipoq)20-22. Under surgical stress, CAR cells can become pro-fibrotic, characterized by the expression of CD20013. In addition to CD200, pro-fibrotic LEPR+ cells also express ACTA2 (αSMA), Tagln (SM22a), and FBLN2 13. Ablation of fibrotic LEPR+ cells leads to a reduction in peri-implant fibrous tissue, while transplantation of fibrotic LEPR+ cells is sufficient to induce the formation of peri-implant fibrous tissue.

Gremlin1 (GREM1) is a secreted antagonist of the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP)-2, -4, and -723. Upregulation of the BMP pathway was previously shown to increase peri-implant osteogenesis and mineralization24, and to increase recruitment of osteoprogenitors to the site of bone remodeling25. BMPs were also shown to impede fibrosis through inhibition of the transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ) pathways26. While the BMP pathway has been shown to contribute toward peri-implant bone formation, its role, particularly the role of the BMP inhibitor GREM1, in the formation of peri-implant fibrotic tissue and its correlation to the fibrotic LEPR+ cells remains to be elucidated.

Here, we show that GREM1 is prominently expressed by the majority of LEPR⁺ cells within peri-implant fibrotic tissue from both patients undergoing revision surgery and our murine model of peri-implant fibrosis. These GREM1⁺ LEPR⁺ cells co-express classical fibrotic markers (Col3a1, S100a4, CD200) as well as osteogenic markers (OSX, BGLAP), suggesting a diverted differentiation trajectory from osteogenesis toward fibrosis. Functional studies reveal that GREM1 expression in LEPR⁺ cells is required for the development of peri-implant fibrosis, as conditional deletion of Grem1 results in a marked reduction in fibrotic tissue and a concomitant increase in peri-implant bone formation. Mechanistically, Grem1 deletion leads to robust upregulation of both BMP and WNT signaling pathways, redirecting LEPR⁺ cells away from a fibrogenic fate and toward osteogenic differentiation. This pathway is mechanistically distinct from our previously described ADGRF5-mediated signaling, which we showed reduces fibrosis and enhances osteogenesis but does not influence BMP or WNT activation. Notably, pharmacologic inhibition of GREM1 with a neutralizing antibody phenocopies the genetic deletion, further supporting the translational potential of targeting GREM1. Together, these findings identify GREM1 as a novel, mechanistically independent from ADGRF5 signaling, and therapeutically actionable target for preventing and reversing peri-implant fibrosis.

---

## Results

GREM1 is robustly expressed by LEPR+ cells in human and murine peri-implant fibrotic tissue
We hypothesized that the BMP pathway played a crucial part in peri-implant bone and fibrous tissue formation. To interrogate BMP-pathway–associated transcriptional changes under regenerative versus fibrotic conditions, we employed a murine tibial implantation system that generates either stable osseous integration27 or mechanically induced fibrotic encapsulation. Stable press-fit implantation reproducibly supported bone integration, whereas implantation into an overdrilled tibial canal introduced micromotion and promoted fibrous interface formation (referred to subsequently as fibrous-integrated surgery). LepR-lineage cells were isolated from both conditions for comparative transcriptomic analysis (Supplementary Figure 1a–b). Among differentially expressed genes, Grem1, a BMP-inhibitor, emerged as a candidate effector gene of interest in regulating the fibrotic activity of LepR-lineage cells in peri-implant fibrotic tissue.

To validate the transcriptomic findings at the protein level, we examined GREM1 expression in interfacial tissue collected from patients undergoing revision arthroplasty for aseptic loosening (Figure 1a–e, Supplementary Figure 2). Clinical diagnosis was supported by radiographic evidence of peri-implant lucency and intraoperative confirmation of mechanical instability. Histologic evaluation of the interface demonstrated a predominance of elongated stromal cells co-expressing LEPR and GREM1 (Figure 1b-d, Supplementary Figure 2) Notably, LEPR⁺ cells within fibrotic tissue displayed robust GREM1 expression, whereas LEPR⁺ cells in adjacent trabecular bone showed minimal GREM1 signal (Figure 1e, Supplementary Figure 2).

The presence of LEPR+ GREM1+ cells in human peri-implant fibrotic tissue led us to question whether LepR-tdTomato+ GREM1+ cells similarly comprised the peri-implant fibrotic tissue in a murine model. Similar to the human peri-implant fibrotic tissue, murine peri-implant fibrotic tissue contained LepR-tdTomato+ spindle-shaped fibroblasts that expressed GREM1 (Figure 1f-j, Supplementary Figure 1c, Supplementary Figure 3). Furthermore, similar to our observations in human fibrous tissue and normal bone, a significantly higher percentage of LepR-tdTomato+ cells in the peri-implant fibrotic tissue expressed GREM1 compared to LepR-tdTomato+ cells in normal peri-implant bone that underwent osseous integration (Figure 1k, Supplementary Figure 1c, Supplementary Figure 3). There was no statistically significant difference in the total percentage of LepR-tdTomato+ cells in the peri-implant fibrous tissue and the peri-implant bone between the inducible CreERT and the constitutionally active Cre (Supplementary Figure 3c-d). Taken together, under homeostatic conditions, LepR-lineage cells did not express GREM1, consistent with a previous study showing that Grem1-lineage cells represent less than 1% of LEPR+ cells21. Under pro-fibrotic conditions, both human and murine peri-implant LepR-lineage cells acquired expression of GREM1.

Periosteal cells minimally contribute to peri-implant fibrosis
To test the possibility that the periosteal stromal cells contributed toward peri-implant fibrotic tissue, we performed fibrous integration surgery on both Gli1-CreERT;tdTomato mice to track Gli1-lineage cells28, and Ctsk-Cre;mTmG to track Ctsk-lineage cells29.

Ctsk-lineage cells were found in the periosteum and endosteal osteoclasts as previously reported29 (Supplementary Figure 4a). However, Ctsk-lineage minimally contributed to the cells in the peri-implant fibrotic tissue (Supplementary Figure 4a), with only around 10 percent of the cells in the peri-implant fibrotic tissue being Ctsk-lineage (Supplementary Figure 4d). Gli1-lineage cells were found in both the periosteum and in the growth plate region, as previously reported (Supplementary Figure 4b)28. However, Gli1-lineage cells minimally contributed to peri-implant fibrotic tissue (Supplementary Figure 4b), with less than 10 percent of cells in the peri-implant fibrous being Gli1-lineage (Supplementary Figure 4d). Taken together, periosteal cells marked by Ctsk or Gli1 lineage reporters only made a minor contribution to peri-implant fibrous tissue, while LepR-lineage cells provided a significantly higher contribution to peri-implant fibrotic tissue.

LepR-lineage skeletal cells in the peri-implant fibrotic tissue express a fibrotic gene signature
The presence of LepR-tdTomato+ cells in the peri-implant fibrotic tissue led us to question whether these fibrotic LepR-tdTomato+ expressed fibrotic signature markers, such as COL3A130 and S100A413. To address this, we performed fibrous integration surgery on both LepR-CreERT;tdTomato;Col3a1-GFP to trace Col3a1-expressing LepR-tdTomato+ cells and LepR-CreERT;tdTomato;S100a4-GFP to trace S100a4-expressing LepR-tdTomato+ cells.

Using genetic reporters for COL3A1 and S100A4, LepR-tdTomato+ cells in the fibrotic tissue could be distinguished from other populations of LepR-tdTomato+ cells by their expression of COL3A1 (Supplementary Figure 5a-e) and S100A4 (Supplementary Figure 6a-e). In contrast, in the osseointegration surgery model, the LepR-tdTomato+ cells in the peri-implant osseous tissue expressed neither COL3A1 (Supplementary Figure 5f-j) nor S100a4 (Supplementary Figure 6f-j). A higher percentage of LepR-lineage cells was found in the peri-implant fibrotic tissue of mice that underwent fibrous integration surgery than in the peri-implant bone tissue of mice that underwent osseointegration surgery (Supplementary Figure 5k, 6k). A higher percentage of LepR-lineage cells in the peri-implant fibrotic tissue expressed COL3A1 and S100A4 than the corresponding LepR-lineage cells in the peri-implant osseous tissue in the osseointegrated press-fit model (Supplementary Figure 5l-m, 6l-m). Col3a1- and S100a4- expressing skeletal LepR-tdTomato+ cells were previously reported to represent the pro-fibrotic population in murine skeletal fibrosis models13,30. Taken together, LepR-lineage cells in the peri-implant fibrotic tissue expressed signature pro-fibrotic genes such as COL3A1 and S100A4, thus assuming a fibrogenic fate.

Fibrotic LepR-tdTomato+ cells express osteogenic markers OSX and BGLAP
We next sought to determine whether LepR-tdTomato+ cells in the peri-implant fibrotic tissue retain expression of osteogenic lineage markers, such as BGLAP31 and OSX32. We hypothesized that during the immediate postoperative period, marrow LepR-tdTomato+ cells expressed early osteogenic markers, such as OSX that would later evolve to include the expression of late osteogenic markers, such as BGLAP. Additionally, we hypothesized that the expression of osteogenic lineage markers by LepR-tdTomato+ cells follows a radial gradient from the endosteal bone, such that LepR-tdTomato+ cells closest to the endosteal bone progress from early to later stages of the osteogenic lineage at earlier time points than those located farther away. To address this question, we performed fibrous-integration surgery on LepR-CreERT;tdTomato;Osx-mCherry mice to trace OSX-expressing LepR-tdTomato+ cells, and LepR-CreERT;tdTomato;Bglap-GFP mice to trace BGLAP-expressing LepR-tdTomato+ cells (Figure 2). To further refine the spatial analysis of these cells and assess osteogenic lineage marker expression as a function of radial distance from the host endosteal bone, we divided the peri-implant fibrous tissue layer into three equal zones of increasing radial distance from the endosteal bone post-drilling. Zone one represented the one-third of the fibrous tissue closest to the host endosteal bone, zone two corresponded to the middle zone of the fibrous tissue, and zone three referred to the one-third of the fibrous tissue closest to the implant (Figure 2a-c).

At postoperative day 3, the peri-implant area consisted of early, disorganized peri-implant fibrotic tissue, which was mostly LepR-tdTomato- (Figure 2a). This early, disorganized peri-implant fibrotic tissue was OSX- (Figure 2a), BGLAP-GFP- (Figure 2g), and GREM1- (Figure 2m, Supplementary Figure 7). At the junction between trabecular bone and the early fibrotic tissue, the marrow space was filled with spindle-shaped LepR-tdTomato+ cells that are OSX+ (Figure 2a), BGLAP+ (Figure 2g), and GREM1+ (Figure 2m, Supplementary Figure 7). The proportion of OSX-expressing LepR-tdTomato+ cells peaked at postoperative day 7 in zones 2 and 3 (Figure 2b, d-f) and then declined at postoperative day 14 (Figure 2c, d-f). The proportion of LepR-tdTomato+ BGLAP+ and LepR-tdTomato+ GREM1+ cells continued to increase from postoperative day 3 to 14 in all zones (Figure 2g-r, Supplementary Figure 7). Taken together, early LepR-tdTomato+ cells in the peri-implant fibrous tissue expressed OSX. Over time, these LepR-tdTomato+ cells ceased expressing OSX and expressed BGLAP and GREM1.

Conditional deletion of Grem1 in LepR-lineage cells attenuated peri-implant fibrosis
To determine whether GREM1 expression in LepR-lineage cells influences peri-implant tissue composition, we conditionally deleted Grem1 in LepR-lineage cells (LepR-Cre;tdTomato;Grem1fl/fl, hereafter called LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f mice). Twelve to sixteen week old LepR-Cre;tdTomato;Grem1fl/fl and LepR-Cre;tdTomato;Grem1+/+ (control, LepR-Cre+) underwent fibrous-integrated surgery and analyzed the interface two weeks following fibrous-integration surgery (Figure 3a). Micro-computed tomography analysis showed a statistically significant increase in peri-implant bone mass in LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f mice compared to LepR-Cre+ control after fibrous-integrated surgery (Figure 3b-d). This finding was further supported by the histomorphometric analysis of the peri-implant tissue, demonstrating a significant reduction in peri-implant fibrosis in LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f mice (Figure 3e-g, Supplementary Figure 8a-h). Micro-computed tomography and histomorphometric analyses of baseline, non-operated tibiae revealed no significant differences in bone mass between LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f and LepR-Cre+ (Supplementary Figure 9). The frequency of Lin- LepR-tdTomato+ cells in LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f mice was significantly decreased compared to LepR-Cre+ controls, as shown by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence (Figure 3h-j). In conjunction with the reduction in peri-implant fibrosis, we also observed a concomitant reduction in the number of fibrosis-associated LepR-tdTomato+ CD200+ cells post fibrous-integrated surgery (Figure 3k-l). The overall increase in the peri-implant bone mass and decrease in the peri-implant fibrous tissue in LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f mice further manifested as an increase in its host bone-implant interface strength as compared to LepR-Cre+ mice (Figure 3m-n). Taken together, conditional deletion of Grem1 in LepR-lineage cells does not affect baseline bone quality but reduces the post-surgical frequency of LepR-lineage cells and consequently attenuates the formation of peri-implant fibrotic tissue.

GREM1 inhibition reduced cell proliferation and skewed cellular differentiation from a fibrogenic towards an osteogenic fate
Given the reduction in fibrotic tissue following Grem1 deletion, we next evaluated whether LepR-lineage cell expansion within the peri-implant niche was dependent on GREM1. To assess cumulative proliferation, we administered bromo-deoxyuridine (BrdU) to 12-16 week-old LepR-Cre;tdTomato;Grem1fl/fl and LepR-Cre;tdTomato;Grem1+/+ mice that underwent fibrous-integration surgery daily for 14 days, starting immediately after surgery (Figure 4a-d). Conditional knockout of Grem1 in LepR-tdTomato+ cells led to a significant decrease in LepR-tdTomato+ cell proliferation in the peri-implant area (Figure 4a-d, o).

To assess whether LepR-tdTomato+ cell-derived GREM1 direct the differentiation of LepR-tdTomato+ cells towards a fibrogenic fate, LepR-tdTomato⁺ cells isolated from from LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f and LepR-Cre+ mice that underwent fibrous-integration surgeries were engrafted intramuscularly into recipient mice (Fig. 4e–n). While LepR-tdTomato+ cells from the LepR-Cre+ donors exclusively formed graft-derived fibrotic tissue after transplantation, LepR-tdTomato+ cells from LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f donors formed bone nodules containing graft-derived osseous and adipose tissue after transplantation (Figure 4e-n). Micro-computed tomography analysis of the mineralized tissue demonstrated a significantly higher amount of mineralized tissue in graft-derived tissue from LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f relative to the graft-derived tissue from LepR-Cre+ control donors (Figure 4p). Taken together, deletion of Grem1 in LepR-lineage cells resulted in a phenotypic switch in differentiation capacity due to cell intrinsic reprogramming.

Conditional deletion of Grem1 in LepR-lineage cells upregulated BMP and WNT Pathways
GREM1 is a member of the differential screening-selected gene aberrative in neuroblastoma (DAN) family of secreted BMP antagonist and selectively binds to BMP-2, -4, and -7 to inhibit BMP pathway signaling33. GREM1 also inhibits WNT signaling, and, accordingly, downregulation of GREM1 resulted in enhanced WNT signaling34. We hypothesized that inhibition of GREM1 in LepR-lineage cells resulted in upregulation of BMP and WNT Pathways, resulting in increased osteogenesis and downregulation of fibrosis.

To define the molecular consequences of Grem1 deletion, we performed transcriptomic analysis of LepR-tdTomato+ cells isolated from LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f and LepR-Cre+ mice that underwent fibrous-integration surgery and subsequent gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA). Principal component analysis (PCA) established that LepR-tdTomato+ cells isolated from LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f and LepR-Cre+ mice displayed distinct transcriptional profiles (Figure 5a). We identified enrichment of genes involved in BMP and WNT pathways in the LepR-tdTomato+ from LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f (Figure 5b-c). BMP4 and BM7, but not BMP2, BMP6, and BMP9 were upregulated in the peri-implant tissue of LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f mice compared to that of LepR-Cre+ mice (Supplementary Figure 10-12). Unlike GREM1, NOGGIN, another BMP-pathway inhibitor, was not significantly expressed by LepR-lineage cells in the peri-implant area (Supplementary Figure 12). Furthermore, phosphorylated SMAD (pSMAD) 1/5/8 and active β-catenin, markers of active BMP and WNT signaling respectively, were upregulated in the peri-implant tissue of LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f mice compared to that of LepR-Cre+ mice (Figure 5d-i). By contrast, conditional deletion of Adgrf5 in LepR-tdTomato⁺ cells had no effect on Grem1 expression—and vice versa, Grem1 knockout did not alter Adgrf5 levels (Supplementary Figure 13)—and neither BMP nor WNT signaling was significantly perturbed in LepR-Cre⁺;Adgrf5f/f animals. These data demonstrate that GREM1, but not ADGRF5, serves as a critical brake on BMP/WNT-driven osteogenesis in the peri-implant niche.

In agreement with our submuscular engraftment result, conditional knockout of Grem1 in LepR-lineage cells resulted in upregulation of pro-osteogenic genes associated with BMP or WNT pathways (e.g. Alx335,36, Bmp737, Bmp438, Acvr2b39,40, Acvr1c41, Wnt2b42, Wnt643, Wnt444, Wnt10a43, Bglap45, and Bglap245, Efemp146,47, Ccn348 , Hoxd1349, Supplementary Figure 14a), upregulation of anti-fibrotic genes associated with BMP or WNT pathways (e.g. Bmp450, Bmp751, Wnt2b52, Wnt453, Wnt654, Klf1555, Pitx256,57, Efemp158, Fgfr459,60, Supplementary Figure 14b), downregulation of anti-osteogenic genes (e.g. Frzb61, Tns362, Nsd263, Panx364, Trpv465, Fgfr366, Osmr67, Lgr668, Icam269, Igf2r70, Supplementary Figure 14c), and downregulation of pro-fibrotic genes (Osmr71, Rasal172, Fzd973, Lgr674, Ets175, Flnb76, Hoxc877, Chst1178,79, Trpv465,80, Nid281, Igf2r82, Supplementary Figure 14d).

In concordance with our BRDU study, conditional knockout of Grem1 in LepR-lineage cells resulted in upregulation of anti-proliferation genes associated with BMP or WNT pathways (e.g. Podn83, Wnt484, Acvr1c85, Bmp486, Bmp787, Efemp158, Inmt88, Hepacam89, Eno390, Dpp491, Supplementary Figure 14e) and downregulation of pro-proliferation genes (e.g. Lgr692, Egfl793, Lef194, Panx395, Apln96, Notch497, Piezo198, Tert99, Stc1100, Dlk2101, Supplementary Figure 14f). Taken together, the deletion of Grem1 in LepR-lineage cells resulted in an upregulation of BMP and WNT pathway-associated osteogenic genes, and downregulation of pro-fibrotic and pro-proliferation genes and represent an orthogonal pathway from the previously reported Adgrf5 axis.

GREM1 blocking antibodies prevent peri-implant fibrosis and improve peri-implant osseointegration
Since conditional genetic deletion of Grem1 in LepR-lineage cells resulted in the reduction of peri-implant fibrosis, we hypothesized that administration of an anti-GREM1 blocking antibody would also prevent peri-implant fibrosis and promote peri-implant osteogenesis, therefore acting as prophylaxis against peri-implant fibrosis. Anti-GREM1 antibodies (previously shown to block GREM1 signaling102) were administered via intra-articular injections from postoperative day 0 to day 14 in LepR-Cre;tdTomato mice undergoing fibrous-integration surgery. (Figure 6a).

After a total of 14 days of treatment, μCT analysis showed an enhancement of peri-implant bone formation in anti-GREM1 treated mice as compared to mice treated with an isotype control (Figure 6b-d). The bone volume over total volume and the trabecular thickness in the peri-implant area were significantly higher relative to controls (Figure 6c-d, Supplementary Figure 8i-j). Histomorphometry analysis further showed a reduction in peri-implant fibrous tissue and an increase in peri-implant bone formation in the anti-GREM1 treated mice as compared to isotype controls (Figure 6e-g). Micro-computed tomography and histomorphometric analyses of the ipsilateral femur revealed no significant differences between mice treated with anti-GREM1 relative to mice receiving an isotype control (Supplementary Figure 15). Finally, flow cytometric analysis and immunofluorescence imaging demonstrated decreased numbers of both LepR-tdTomato+ and LepR-tdTomato+CD200+ cells in the peri-implant area of anti-GREM1 treated mice (Figure 6h-l). The overall increase in the peri-implant bone mass and decrease in the peri-implant fibrous tissue as seen in the microCT and histomorphometric analysis further manifests as an increase in bone-implant interface-strength, as compared to control mice (Figure 6m-n).

GREM1-blocking antibodies treat established peri-implant fibrosis
We then asked whether administration of anti-GREM1 can promote remodeling of established peri-implant fibrosis back into an osseus interface and, therefore, act as a treatment. To address this question, we administered anti-GREM1 starting from postoperative week 2 until postoperative week 4 to LepR-Cre;tdTomato that underwent fibrous-integrated surgery (Figure 7a).

Micro-computed tomography analysis showed an enhancement of peri-implant bone formation in anti-GREM1 treated mice as compared to mice treated with isotype control (Figure 7b-d). The bone volume over total volume and trabecular number in the peri-implant area were significantly higher relative to controls, while the trabecular spacing in the peri-implant area was significantly lower relative to controls (Figure 7c-d, f). Histomorphometric analysis further showed a significant reduction in peri-implant fibrous tissue and an increase in peri-implant bone formation in the anti-GREM1 treated mice as compared to isotype controls (Figure 7e, g-h, Supplementary Figure 9k-l). Micro-computed tomography and histomorphometric analyses of the ipsilateral femur revealed no significant differences between mice treated with anti-GREM1 relative to mice receiving an isotype control (Supplementary Figure 16). Flow cytometry analysis and immunofluorescence imaging demonstrated decreased numbers of both LepR-tdTomato+ and LepR-tdTomato+CD200+ cells in the peri-implant area of anti-GREM1 treated mice (Figure 7h-m). The overall increase in the peri-implant bone mass and decrease in the peri-implant fibrous tissue, as seen in the microCT and histomorphometric analysis, further manifested as an increase in host bone-implant interface-strength as compared to control mice (Figure 7n-o). Taken together, these results provided proof-of-principle that inhibition of GREM1 is a promising strategy to not only prevent but also to treat established peri-implant fibrosis.

## Methods

Institutional approvals
All procedures were carried out in accordance with applicable ethical and regulatory requirements. Animal experiments followed NIH guidelines for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the Weill Cornell Medicine Subcommittee on Animal Care (IACUC protocol 2018-0001). Procurement and use of human specimens were performed under approval from the Hospital for Special Surgery Institutional Review Board (IRB protocol 2019-0571), which included HIPAA authorization, and all study conduct adhered to ethical principles consistent with the 2008 Declaration of Helsinki. The IRB permitted the use of de-identified residual clinical specimens under a waiver of informed consent; accordingly, written informed consent was not required.

Animals
Lepr-cre (Stock 008320), Rosa26-CAG-loxp-stop-loxp-tdTomato (Stock 007909), Rosa26-CAG-loxp-stop-loxp-iDTR (Stock 007900), S100a4-GFP (Stock 012893), NSG-EGFP (Stock 021937) mice were obtained from Jackson Laboratories. Col3a1-GFP (Stoc 010616-UCD) mice was obtained from Mutant Mouse Resource & Research Centers (MMRRC). LepR-CreERT mice were provided by Bo Zhou (Chinese Academy of Sciences, China). Grem1fl/fl mice were a gift from Aris Economides (Regeneron, USA). All mice were maintained on a C57BL/6 background and housed/handled in compliance with NIH guidelines for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals under protocols approved by the Weill Cornell Medical College Subcommittee on Animal Care (IACUC). For antibody studies, mice were randomized to receive anti-GREM1 versus isotype control. Microcomputed tomography (μCT) analyses were performed with blinding to experimental condition. Unless otherwise indicated, CreER recombination was induced by daily intraperitoneal tamoxifen injections for three consecutive days administered two weeks before surgery. Experiments used 10–18-week-old mice, with a minimum of 3 animals per experiment. Both male and female animals were included and randomized when assigned to groups. Post hoc sex-based statistical comparisons were not performed due to low sample size; sex-disaggregated values are provided in the Source Data.

Animal welfare and euthanasia
Animals were housed in an AAALAC-accredited, specific pathogen–free facility under standard conditions with ad libitum access to food and water, along with environmental enrichment. Trained personnel assessed mice at least daily and more frequently after surgery; monitoring included body condition, weight trends, mobility/limb use, grooming, and surgical-site integrity. Peri-operative analgesia and supportive care were delivered per institutional veterinary recommendations and the approved IACUC protocol. Humane endpoints—including >15–20% weight loss, persistent distress, impaired ambulation, or wound complications—prompted veterinary evaluation and, when indicated, early euthanasia. Euthanasia was performed by CO₂ inhalation with a secondary physical method (e.g., cervical dislocation) to confirm death, consistent with institutional practice, AVMA guidance, and IACUC protocol 2018-0001.

Human specimens
Human specimen use was approved under the Hospital for Special Surgery IRB protocol 2019-0571, which included HIPAA authorization and conduct consistent with the 2008 Declaration of Helsinki. The IRB allowed use of de-identified residual clinical material under a waiver of informed consent; therefore, written informed consent was not required. Peri-implant fibrous interface tissue was collected from 9 patients (5 males and 4 females, 40–85 years old) undergoing revision arthroplasty 2–10 years after primary total hip or total knee replacement for aseptic loosening; specimens analyzed were not required for clinical management. Patients revised for septicemia were excluded using Musculoskeletal Infection Society criteria107. Aseptic loosening was confirmed by radiographic peri-implant lucency and intraoperative evidence of a mechanically loose implant together with peri-implant fibrotic tissue on operative assessment. Interface tissue was harvested by blunt scraping of fibrotic tissue adjacent to the implant from the proximal femur or acetabulum in total hip arthroplasty cases, and from the distal femur or proximal tibia in total knee arthroplasty cases. Harvested specimens comprised predominantly fibrous tissue with a small amount of underlying bone, enabling assessment of both bone-to-fibrous tissue and implant-to-fibrous tissue interfaces. Control “normal bone” samples were obtained from 4 patients (2 males and 2 females, 50–73 years old) undergoing primary total hip arthroplasty (greater trochanter region) or primary total knee arthroplasty (proximal tibia). Sex- or gender-based analyses were not performed due to limited sample size. Identifying patient information was removed at the time of procurement.

Fibrous integration surgery
Mice were anesthetized with isoflurane delivered by nose cone (2% isoflurane, 2 L/min) and surgery was performed under sterile technique. An ~8 mm medial parapatellar incision was made in the operative knee. The quadriceps fibers were released medially to permit lateral subluxation of the patella and exposure of the tibial plateau. The anterior cruciate ligament was released at its tibial insertion and both menisci were excised. Using a fine-tip burr, articular cartilage and the proximal epiphysis were removed down to the level of the posterior cruciate ligament insertion. To model an end-stage aseptic loosening phenotype—specifically, formation of a fibrous interface between implant and host bone—a 1.4 mm diameter × 2.0 mm length hole was created in the medullary canal. A medical-grade poly(methyl methacrylate) implant (Simplex P, Stryker, New Jersey, USA) was inserted until its top surface was flush with the proximal tibia. The implant articulating surface measured 2.0 mm (major axis) × 1.5 mm (minor axis) with a thickness of 0.2 mm; the stem measured 2.0 mm in length and 1.0 mm in diameter. Knee range of motion was verified before closure. The extensor mechanism and skin were closed in layers using resorbable sutures. Postoperative analgesia was provided with buprenorphine (0.05 mg/kg subcutaneously) for the first 48 hours. Mice were allowed full weight bearing and unrestricted activity from the day of surgery until sacrifice.

Osseointegration surgery
Osseointegration surgery used the same exposure and initial preparation as fibrous integration surgery, with the following changes. After cartilage and proximal epiphysis removal, a 10.9 mm diameter × 2.0 mm length hole was created in the medullary canal. A direct metal laser sintered implant composed of medical-grade Ti6Al4V alloy was press-fit into the prepared cavity until flush with the proximal tibial surface. The dimensions of the implant articulating surface were 2.0 mm for the major axis and 1.5 mm for the minor axis, with a 0.2 mm thickness. The stem was 2.0 mm in length and 1.0 mm in diameter. Closure was performed as described above. Buprenorphine (0.05 mg/kg subcutaneously) was administered for the first 48 hours postoperatively. Animals were permitted full weight bearing and no activity restriction from surgery to sacrifice.

Isolation of mesenchymal cells
The proximal tibia (2 mm from the most proximal surface) was processed using combined mechanical disruption and enzymatic digestion. Tissue was minced with sterile scissors and digested at 37°C with constant agitation for up to 45 minutes in digestion buffer containing collagenase P (1 mg/ml; Roche, cat 11213857001) and dispase II (2 mg/ml; Roche, cat 04942078001). The reaction was quenched by adding α-minimum essential medium (αMEM) supplemented with 2% serum, followed by centrifugation to pellet cells. After removing the supernatant, pellets were resuspended in DNase I (2 units/ml) and incubated for 10 minutes at 37°C. αMEM with 2% serum was added, samples were triturated thoroughly, filtered through a 70 μm nylon mesh, and centrifuged again. The final pellet was used for fluorescence-assisted cell sorting (FACS).

Fluorescence-assisted cell sorting (FACS)
Single-cell suspensions were washed twice in ice-cold FACS buffer consisting of 2% FBS and 1 mM EDTA in PBS. Cells were then blocked for 30 minutes at 4°C using blocking buffer (1:100 dilution; BD Bioscience 553142). Antibodies were diluted in Brilliant Stain Buffer (BD Bioscience, 563794), and samples were incubated with primary antibody mixtures for 40 minutes at 4°C in the dark. Cells were washed twice with FACS buffer, followed by additional washes, and resuspended in FACS buffer containing DAPI (4–6 diamidino-2-phenylindole; 1 μg/ml; BD Bioscience, 564907). Sorting/acquisition was performed on a Becton Dickinson Aria II equipped with 5 lasers (BD Bioscience). Initial compensation was set using compensation beads (Invitrogen, 01-3333-42), then refined using fluorescence-minus-one (FMO) controls, which were also used to define background for each fluorophore. Gates distinguishing positive and negative populations were established using internal FMO controls. For each analysis, ~1–2.5 million events were typically collected. Data were analyzed in FlowJo (version 10.6); calculations were performed in Excel, and plots were generated in GraphPad Prism. Gating strategies are provided in Supplementary Figure 19.

FACS antibodies
For mouse flow cytometry, antibodies included CD45 (clone 30-F11, BD Bioscience), CD31 (clone MEC13.3, BD Bioscience), and Ter119 (clone Ter119, BD Biosciences). Flow cytometry was performed using a FACS Aria II (BD Biosciences).

Intramuscular engraftment
Intramuscular transplantation was carried out in 4–8-week-old NSG-eGFP mice (Stock 021937). A ~1 mm anterolateral incision was created on the right hindlimb to expose the right quadriceps. The quadriceps muscle complex was gently dissected and a 2–3 mm intramuscular pouch was formed. A Surgifoam absorbable gelatin sponge (Ethicon, 1972) loaded with the sorted cell population of interest was placed into the pouch. The site was closed in two layers to ensure full encapsulation of the sponge: first the fascial layer and then the skin. Bone nodules were harvested 8 weeks after implantation.

Transplanted cells were derived from FACS-sorted LepR-tdTomato+ cells isolated from the proximal tibia of LepR-Cre+;Grem1f/f and LepR-Cre+ mice following fibrous integration surgery. To obtain 5,000–10,000 cells per recipient mouse, 5–10 proximal tibiae from operated donor mice were collected on postoperative day 14.

Mechanical testing
Bone–implant interface strength was assessed by pullout testing as described previously108. After tibial isolation, the distal tibia was embedded in polymethylmethacrylate. The proximal tibia was carefully dissected to enable a custom fixture to clamp the implant beneath its plateau. The implant long axis was aligned with the pullout direction, and testing was performed on an EnduraTEC ELF3200 system (Bose, EdenPrairie, Minnesota). Implants were extracted at 0.03 mm/sec until complete removal. The peak pullout load (N) was obtained from the resulting load–displacement curves.

Intra-articular administration of an GREM1-blocking antibody
Neutralizing anti-GREM1 was administered intra-articularly to LepR-Cre;tdTomato mice undergoing fibrous integration surgery; the antibody has been previously shown to neutralize GREM1 activity102. In the prevention paradigm, dosing was performed twice weekly from postoperative day 0 through day 14 (Figure 4a). For treatment of established peri-implant fibrosis, dosing was performed twice weekly from postoperative day 14 through day 28 (Figure 5a). Each injection delivered 10 μL of a 10 μg/mL solution of anti-GREM1 (LSBio, LS-C125371) or isotype control (Abcam, ab91353) diluted in PBS. Prior to injecting, residual unbound antibody was aspirated.

For intra-articular delivery, mice were anesthetized with isoflurane by nose cone (2% isoflurane, 2 L/min). The skin was prepared with diluted povidone–iodine and allowed to dry. With the knee held at ~45° flexion, a sterile 26-gauge needle attached to an empty 10 μL syringe (Hamilton, CAL7635) was inserted just lateral to the patellar tendon and just superior to the tibial joint line. Synovial fluid was aspirated to create space. While maintaining needle position intra-articularly, the empty syringe was replaced with a second 10 μL syringe containing antibody or isotype, and the solution was injected into the joint.

Sample preparation for cryosectioning
Freshly harvested tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) at 4°C for 6 hours, washed in PBS, and decalcified in 0.5 M EDTA for 8 days. Samples were then transferred to infiltration solution (20% sucrose + 2% PVP) and rocked until they sank. Specimens were embedded in OCT containing 15% sucrose and stored at −80°C. Sections (15 μm thick) were cut using a Leica cryostat.

To verify that implant removal after EDTA decalcification did not artifactually disrupt peri-implant tissue architecture, we compared histomorphometric outcomes between specimens in which the implant was removed post-decalcification and specimens processed without decalcification with the implant retained (Supplementary Figure 8). No statistically significant differences were detected in peri-implant fibrosis or peri-implant bone between these approaches (Supplementary Figure 8).

Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
Frozen sections were brought to room temperature and thawed for 10 minutes, rehydrated in PBS for 20 minutes, and permeabilized with 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS for 15 minutes. Sections were then blocked in 5% donkey serum (PBS) before incubation with primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer (overnight, 4 °C). After PBS washes, fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:400) were applied, followed by nuclear counterstaining with 4’,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) (300 nM) for 10 minutes and mounting in antifade medium (Life Technologies, P36970). Confocal imaging was performed on a Zeiss LSM 880 with Airyscan using ZEN 2.3 software. Isotype controls were included to ensure minimum background signal, and image processing/quantification was performed using Carl Zeiss Zen 2.3 SP1 FP3 (black, v14.0.18.201, Germany).

Primary antibodies for IHC
Primary antibodies used for immunofluorescence included murine LEPR (R&D System, AF497, 1:100 dilution), human LEPR (R&D system, MAB867), GREM1 (LSBio, LS-C125371, 1:100 dilution), murine CD200 (Abcam, ab33734, 1:100 dilution), mouse active-β-Catenin (Milipore Sigma, 05-665, clone 8E7, 1:100 dilution), phospho Smad1/Smad5/Smad8 (EMD Milipore, AB3848-I, 1:100 dilution), Noggin (R&D System, AF719, 1:100 dilution), BMP2 (Abcam, ab214821, 1:100 dilution), BMP4 (Abcam, ab39973, 1:100 dilution), BMP6 (R&D System, AF6325, 1:100 dilution), BMP7 (Bioss USA, bs-2242R, 1:100 dilution), BMP9 (R&D System, MAB3209, 1:100 dilution).

Histological quantification
H&E staining were performed following the recommended protocol by the kit manufacturer (Abcam, ab245880), and whole-slide images were analyzed in QuPath109 (version 0.4.4). For each section, a peri-implant region of interest was defined as a 200 µm band extending outward from the implant interface. A supervised random-trees pixel classifier was trained to segment bone, fibrous tissue, and marrow/fat using manual annotations across multiple representative slides until performance was visually consistent. The trained classifier was then applied to the ROI for each sample, and segmented classes were converted to annotations to compute area fractions for each tissue compartment.

μCT scanning and analysis
Murine bones were scanned using a Scanco µCT 35 (6 µm isotropic voxel size; 55 kVp; 0.145 mA; 600 ms integration; 0.36° step over 180°, SCANCO Medical, Bassersdorf, Switzerland) while submerged in PBS108. Reconstructions were segmented to delineate implant, mineralized bone, and the radiolucent interfacial region. A peri-implant volume of interest was defined as a 200 µm shell extending outward from the segmented implant surface (Supplementary Figure 18). Standard trabecular metrics were computed in Scanco software following published guidelines outlined by Bouxsein et al., 2010110, including BV/TV and trabecular microarchitecture (trabecular thickness (Tb.Th), trabecular separation (Tb.Sp), and mean trabecular number (Tb.N)). Trabecular thickness, mean trabecular separation, and mean trabecular number were derived using sphere-fitting approaches implemented by the vendor. For trabecular thickness, spheres were fitted to the object, and for separation, spheres were fitted to the background111. Analyses were performed blinded to genotype/treatment.

Bulk RNA sequencing
LEPR+ cells were FACS-purified from the murine peri-implant region at postoperative day 14. RNA was isolated using the RNeasy Micro Kit (Qiagen, Germantown, MD, USA) and used for library preparation with the Illumina TruSeq RNA Sample Preparation workflow. Libraries were sequenced to ~15–25 million single-end reads per sample using HiSeq2500 with 50-bp single-end reads. Adapters and low-quality bases were removed with fastp112., and reads were aligned to the mouse reference genome (mm10) with STAR using Gencode v27 annotations for exon counting113.. Differential expression was assessed in R using edgeR (quasi-likelihood framework). Differential expression analysis was performed using the DESeq2 package and visualized in R using Shiny-driven visualization platform (RNAseq DRAMA, https://gitlab.com/hssgenomics/Shiny).

Statistical analyses
Data are reported as mean ± standard deviation (S.D.) or standard error of the mean (S.D.), as specified in each legend. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test where applicable. Two-group comparisons were performed using unpaired, two-tailed Student’s t-tests for normally distributed data or Mann–Whitney tests otherwise. For ≥3 groups, one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test was used when assumptions were met; otherwise, Kruskal–Wallis testing followed by Dunn’s correction was applied. Analyses were performed in GraphPad PRISM software (v8.4.3, La Jolla, CA). P < 0.05 was considered significant.

Data Availability
The main data supporting the results in this study are available in the paper and supplementary information. The raw and analyzed data generated during the study are available for research purposes from the corresponding author within reasonable request. Transcriptomic data from bulk RNA-seq has been deposited at the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession numbers GSE313854 and GSE227869. Source data are provided with this paper.

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript by Suhardi and colleagues addresses the problem of fibrous encapsulation, e.g., where an implant loosens and becomes encased in a fibrous tissue envelope rather than bone. The causes of fibrous encapsulation range from biological to physical e.g., excessive/early loading; consequently, there is clinical value in understanding at least part of the etiological basis for fibrous encapsulation.
The authors show evidence that LepR+ cells contribute to peri-implant fibrotic tissue, and that Grem1 is expressed in the same location. They then provide data showing that knockout of Grem1 leads to enhanced WNT and BMP signaling and associated downstream events including osteogenic differentiation. The daily delivery of an anti-GREM1 antibody appears to reduce the formation of fibrous tissue even in a femoral implant that is placed into an oversized osteotomy. This is an important finding because it suggests that a biological factor can override the role of physical forces/excessive micromotion that typically results in fibrous encapsulation. Fibrous encapsulation can also be reversed by delivery of the anti-GREM1 antibody, leading the authors to postulate that a anti-GREM1-mediated therapy may be of value in reducing the incidence of fibrous encapsulation.
This proposed therapeutic strategy, however, does not take into account the fact that implant loosening is a gradual process and its onset varies depending on factors such as implant type, surgical technique, etc. To employ an anti-GREM1 antibody strategy as a preventative would require extensive safety data demonstrating that manipulation of BMP and WNT pathways holds no short- or long-term safety issues. This important point is not discussed.
Nonetheless, the paper makes some important strides in understanding the molecular mechanisms of fibrous encapsulation around femoral (not dental) implants and in this limited application, presents an important but potentially incremental advance in the field of orthopedics.
Major technical limitations
1. In patients, early fibrous encapsulation is often associated with early/excessive loading of the implant. The effect of excessive micromotion is thought to produce strains and stresses in the peri-implant bone that cause it to break down and the bone tissue is then replaced by fibrous tissue. This sequence of events is not replicated in the murine fibrous integration surgery. Instead, fibrous encapsulation is ensured because the implant is undersized relative to the diameter of the osteotomy (1.0mm in diameter for the implant and 1.4mm in diameter for the osteotomy). Consequently, the implant is “floating” in the hole.
2. The implant used in the fibrous encapsulation surgeries is unlikely to w undergo osseointegration because it is fabricated from PMMA and not titanium. There are no threads on the implant used; consequently, it is impossible to ascertain whether we’re looking at the actual tissue-implant interface, as those shown in Fig. 3e. If there was fibrous tissue in zone 3, this could easily be lost during tissue processing.
3. Fig. 3: “we conditionally deleted Grem1 in LepR-lineage cells); when was the deletion performed relative to the fibrous integration surgery? This information is not presented in the Methods section. If, for example, Grem1 was inactivated prior to surgery this could explain the significant increase in BV/TV, Tb.N, Tb.S, etc., unrelated to the surgical procedure. Since there is no mention of when Grem1 is inactivated it is not possible to answer this question.
4. Fig. 4: the authors write that they delivered BrdU “for 14 days, starting immediately after surgery”. This is confusing because it suggests that BrdU was delivered repeatedly. Perhaps they mean that they delivered BrdU once, and traced the BrdU+ cells for 14 days? In any case, the extent of red positive cells is striking. If these represented cells that were proliferating immediately after surgery then there is apparently no turnover e.g., apoptosis and instead widespread proliferation. I have trouble reconciling that interpretation with most existing data that suggest extensive necrosis and apoptosis immediately after surgery, with proliferation only beginning ~72h after surgery.
5. The authors begin by mentioning the number of dental implants and orthopedic placed, and the incidence/prevalence of failure due to aseptic loosening. This gives the false impression that all implants are somehow equal. While implants placed in the oral cavity and those placed in the appendicular skeleton can both undergo fibrous encapsulation and failure, comparative studies have clearly demonstrated that the molecular and cellular mechanisms of soft and hard tissue integration in the oral cavity and in the long bones are distinct and separable processes. Consequently, an investigation of the etiological basis for loosening of femoral implants should limit the rationale for undertaking the study to the type of implants actually examined e.g., orthopedic implants.
Minor technical limitations
1. Fig. 2 shows that bone ingrowth occurs around the implant between post-op day 3-14; what might the interface look like if it was examined on post-op day 30?
2. The magnification of Fig. 2m, lower panel does not appear to be correct. The image shows the entire field from the bone to the implant surface. Also¬, there seems to be very little overlap between Grem1 and LepR. This does not align with the quantification data, however, which indicates a significance of 0.0001.
3. Fig. 3, panel b: the pseudo-colored image superimposed on the micro-CT data obscures what looks like mineralized tissue in the region that is supposedly fibrous tissue.
4. In Fig. 3, panel e: a histologic stain that distinguishes bone from fibrous tissue should be used rather than H&E.
5. In Fig. 3 the authors show expression of CD200 and indicate in the Introduction that it is a marker of skeletal progenitor cells (line 49) then later (line 54) state that CD200 is a marker of fibrosis. Other data indicate it is an immune regulatory molecule. Given the multitude of functions assigned, this does not seem to be a good indicator of fibrosis. I would suggest the use of fibronectin or another well-defined fibrosis marker.
6. Figure 4: the authors refer to the transplantation of LepR cells into a muscle pouch as an “osseous organoid”. Organoids are generally agreed to be three-dimensional cellular structures that are derived from tissue-specific stem cells and grown in vitro. What the authors show instead is a bone nodule. The histology shown is not indicative of bone, cartilage and fat staining. Positive controls should be included so readers understand the histologic appearance of the tissues.
7. Figure 6: please clarify that the anti-GREM1 antibodies were delivered daily for 2 weeks. Please include data demonstrating that the anti-GREM1 used here is a function-blocking antibody.

### Reviewer 2

It is very exciting to see this kind of manuscript in the field of implantology that was dominated by biomechanics, engineering, and cellular biology. The vast majority of existing papers are descriptive in nature.
This study has many strengths such as identification of therapeutic targets in the human pathology implant loosening membranes, development of animal models with intact and mutant Grem1 function, neutralizing antibody treatments, and comparative transcriptomic analysis. The mouse animal model is rigorously analyzed by multiple IHC and quantitative microCT.
This study seems to be the first comprehensive mechanistic study that entailed the verification of Grem1 expression in LEPR+ cells in human tissue, and then replication aseptic loosening in clinically relevant wild type and mutant mice, therapeutic intervention using Grem1 neutralizing antibody, and further screening experiments for future experiments. All these features are exceptional strengths because literature on peri-implant fibrosis and loosening are at the cellular descriptive level. Loss of Grem1 function in the context of peri-implant osseous-integration changes the proliferation and tissue differentiation of the LEPR+ cells. To this end, one additional ‘Figure’ (Diagram or Cartoon) that explains the mechanism of peri-implant fibrosis, osseous integration, and proliferation of peri-implant cells would help readers understand the key concepts and therapeutic intervention. Obviously, this would not require any additional experiments. In the discussion section, please add or clarify whether Grem1 is a secreted protein that affects adjacent cells for differentiation into fibrous vs osteogenic cells (paracrine) or alters intracellular signaling for fibrous/osteogenic phenotypic changes (autocrine). Excessive osteoclastic bone resorption is another mechanism of aseptic loosening. If not, please add sentences in the discussion that the focus of this study is about the diversion of the peri-implant skeletal stem cells into fibrous tissues and osteogenic tissues. Please also mention that osteoclastic bone resorption around the implant is triggered and aggravated by wear particles. In the animal model that was used in this experiment, wear-particle related inflammation and osteoclast formation was not relevant.
Overall, the study is outstanding by unraveling the molecular mechanism of peri-implant fibrosis by highly mechanistic experiments using genetic loss-of-function and neutralizing antibody in a clinically relevant animal model.

### Reviewer 4

General comments: The MS by Suhardi et al reports that exuberant expression of GREM1 by Lepr+ cells drives fibrosis and the expense of osteogenesis at sites of implant placement into bone and that reducing GREM1 via local injection of neutralizing antibody reduces fibrosis and enhances osteogenesis. As peri implant fibrosis is a significant clinical problem and treatment with GREM1 neutralizing antibody is a simple clinical procedure, these findings may be of high impact. However, as presented the data raise concerns about the variable nature of the response to GREM1 antibody treatment in mice (see below for specifics) and that, coupled with the small number of human samples assayed for the presence of GREM1 (n=4 with a wide age range) at sites of peri implant fibrosis, raise concerns about the therapeutic potential of these findings. Additionally, the authors published a very similar finding in 2024 by targeting ADGRF5 in the same Lepr+ cell population but do not compare their new findings to these already published studies, raising concerns about the significance of targeting any one gene product as a therapeutic approach to peri-implant fibrosis and reducing the overall novelty of the current study.
Specific comments:
1. Line 85: there seems to be a sentence missing about the identification of GREM1.
2. Materials and methods: there is a description of isolation of mesenchymal cells from bone, but it is unclear if the cells retrieved include a heterogeneous population including periosteal cells, trabecular and cortical bone osteoblasts and bone marrow. As the number and types of Lepr+ cells would change as a function of age and health status in patients, it is unclear what this mixed population is a model of.
2. Figures would benefit from inclusion of a representative histology section that allows the reader to orient to the immunolocalizations. It is hard to gauge how representative the areas focused on in the panels are in relation to the actual overall histology. This is especially important for the figures (2 and3) where comparisons are being made along the surface of the implant-tissue interfaces.
3. Discussion:
a)The authors suggest that Lepr+ cells need to initiate osteogenesis to produce GREM1 and state that GREM1 expression blocks osteogenesis. It isn't clear from this model why GREM1 would be constantly on if osteogenesis is not occurring. No mention is made about what specifically regulates GREM1 expression in the Lepr+ cells. It is also unclear if all Lepr+ cells have equal ability to become osteoblasts and produce GREM1.
b) No mention is made about how stable the rescue of osteogenesis is with injection of the GREM1 antibody. How does the antibody disrupt the feedback loop between osteoblast differentiation and GREM1 production and what happens when the antibody is no longer present as would be the case for treating patients?
c) The authors state that both the BMP and Wnt pathways are enhanced when GREM1 is blocked but do not discuss which of these signals is required for the reinitiating of osteogenesis.
d) The authors do not address how current findings with blocking GREM1 compare to those they reported in 2024, in the same animal model, of blocking ADGRF5. As the authors claimed anti ADGFR5 therapy was efficacious, it is incumbent upon them to show why additional therapy to block GREM1 is necessary and provides better results than blocking ADGFR5
